introduction.p: described surfaces by equations: x^2+y^2+z^2=9, \qquad z=x^2-y^2, \qquad F(x,y,z)=c. An equation tells us which points belong to a surface. But it does not tell us how to locate a point using two inputs or draw a coordinate grid on it.

A curve used one parameter: \mathbf r(t). The surface-coordinate descriptions in this chapter use two: \mathbf r(u,v). One parameter can move a point along a curve. Two parameters can move a point across a sheet.

subsection.title: Two parameters locate a point
subsection.p: Start with a round pipe of radius 2 and height 5. A point on the pipe can be described by two choices: \text{angle around the pipe},\qquad \text{height along the pipe}. Let the angle be \theta and the height be z. Then \mathbf r(\theta,z) = (2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), \qquad 0\le \theta\le2\pi,\quad 0\le z\le5.

If we hold z fixed, the point moves around a circle: \theta\mapsto (2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z). If we hold \theta fixed, the point moves up a vertical line: z\mapsto (2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z). The surface is made by letting both motions happen.

statement.p: In the cylinder formula above, explain what changes when you vary only the angle, and what changes when you vary only the height. Why are two input numbers useful for specifying a point on this pipe?

hint.p: On the pipe you can change the angle and the height independently, so it takes two numbers to say where you are. How many independent ways can you move along a single curve?

figure.caption: The rectangle of parameter values is wrapped into a cylinder.

subsection.title: Parameter domain and image

statement.p: A parametrization for the sheets considered here is a continuous map \mathbf r:D\to\mathbb R^3, where D is a region in the uv-plane. We write \mathbf r(u,v)=\bigl(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)\bigr). The image of the parametrization is the set of points \{\mathbf r(u,v):(u,v)\in D\}.

subsection.p: The region D is called the parameter domain. It might be a rectangle, a disk, a triangle, or some other region.

We often use the same phrase parametric surface for both the map \mathbf r(u,v) and the geometric surface it traces. When the distinction matters, we will say parametrization for the map and surface for the image.

Here continuity means that small changes of the two inputs produce small changes of the output point; Chapter 6 makes that precise. Continuity alone does not ensure a sheet: \mathbf r(u,v)=(u,0,0) collapses to a line and \mathbf r(u,v)=(0,0,0) to a point. Our present examples describe sheets; later regularity conditions will identify nondegenerate differentiable patches.

statement.p: Keep \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z). The domain 0\le\theta\le2\pi, z\in\mathbb R describes the whole infinite cylinder. Restricting to 1\le z\le4 gives a shorter band. Restricting also to 0\le\theta\le\pi gives its half with y\ge0, since \sin\theta\ge0 on that interval.

On the original pipe, direct substitution gives \mathbf r(0,0)=(2,0,0),\quad \mathbf r(\pi/2,3)=(0,2,3),\quad \mathbf r(\pi/3,2)=(1,\sqrt3,2). The input pair is a point in the parameter domain; the output triple is a point in space.

example.title: A discontinuous rule is not a sheet

statement.p: Define \mathbf r(u,v)= \begin{cases} (u,v,0), \amp u\lt 0,\\ (u,v,1), \amp u\ge0, \end{cases} on the square -1\le u\le1,\qquad -1\le v\le1. The left half of the square is sent to the plane z=0, while the right half is sent to the plane z=1. Along u=0, the image jumps upward by one unit.
This is not one continuous surface patch. It is two half-sheets separated by a tear.

subsection.title: Graphs as parametrized surfaces
subsection.p: For a continuous function f, the graph z=f(x,y) has a natural parametrization: \mathbf r(u,v)=(u,v,f(u,v)). The parameters are just the input coordinates.

example.title: A bowl as a parametrized surface

statement.p: Consider the elliptic bowl z=4-\frac{x^2}{9}-\frac{y^2}{4}. Using x=u,\qquad y=v, we get \mathbf r(u,v) = \left( u,\, v,\, 4-\frac{u^2}{9}-\frac{v^2}{4} \right). If we use all pairs (u,v), this traces the whole paraboloid. If we restrict the domain, for example to -3\le u\le3,\qquad -2\le v\le2, we get only a rectangular patch of the bowl.

subsection.p: This is one reason parametrizations are useful. The same formula can describe a whole surface or only a chosen piece of it, depending on the parameter domain.

A plane from Chapter 1 is also a parametrized surface: \mathbf r(u,v)=P+u\mathbf a+v\mathbf b. Here \mathbf a and \mathbf b must be linearly independent. The parameters are the scalar multiples of the two plane directions.

example.title: An affine plane as a parametrized surface

statement.p: Let P=(1,0,2),\qquad \mathbf a=(2,1,0),\qquad \mathbf b=(0,1,3). Then \mathbf r(u,v) = (1,0,2)+u(2,1,0)+v(0,1,3). So \mathbf r(u,v)=(1+2u,\;u+v,\;2+3v). This is the plane through P spanned by the directions \mathbf a and \mathbf b.

subsection.p: The formula P+u\mathbf a+v\mathbf b describes the whole plane when both parameters range over all real numbers. For the example above, substituting the coordinate formulas into 3x-6y+2z=7 verifies its plane equation.

subsection.title: Coordinate grids on surfaces
subsection.p: A parametrization does more than trace points. It brings a grid with it.
For a surface \mathbf r(u,v), there are two natural families of curves.

If we hold u=u_0 fixed, we get the curve v\mapsto \mathbf r(u_0,v). If we hold v=v_0 fixed, we get the curve u\mapsto \mathbf r(u,v_0). These are called coordinate curves or grid curves. They are entire curves on the surface, not vectors attached to one point.

definition.title: Grid curves on a parametrized surface

statement.p: For a parametrized surface \mathbf r(u,v), the curves \mathbf r(u_0,v) and \mathbf r(u,v_0) are called the grid curves of the parametrization.

subsection.p: On the cylinder \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), the grid curves are easy to see.
Holding z fixed gives horizontal circles. Holding \theta fixed gives vertical lines.
On a sphere, the same idea becomes latitude and longitude.

example.title: Latitude and longitude as grid curves

statement.p: The sphere of radius 3 can be parametrized by \mathbf r(\theta,\phi) = (3\sin\phi\cos\theta,\, 3\sin\phi\sin\theta,\, 3\cos\phi), where 0\le\theta\le2\pi,\qquad 0\le\phi\le\pi. Here \theta goes around the z-axis, and \phi measures angle down from the positive z-axis.
If 0\lt\phi\lt\pi is fixed, then z=3\cos\phi is fixed, and the point moves around a circle of latitude.
If \theta is fixed, then the point moves along a meridian from the north pole to the south pole.

subsection.title: Repeated points, seams, and collapsed edges
subsection.p: The spherical parametrization also shows a small warning. At \phi=0 all values of \theta give the same point: (0,0,3). At \phi=\pi, all values of \theta give (0,0,-3). Also, \theta=0 and \theta=2\pi trace the same meridian. So the parametrization is not one-to-one on the full parameter rectangle.

That is not a mistake. Many useful parametrizations repeat some points. The important thing is to notice when it happens. A collapsed parameter edge does not by itself mean that the geometric surface has a sharp point: the sphere is round even at its poles.

subsection.title: Choosing and checking a parametrization
subsection.p: Start with the shape: use angle and height for a cylinder, two angles for a sphere, and the two input coordinates for a graph. Then check both the formula and its domain. Substitution shows that the output satisfies the desired equation; the parameter ranges tell you which points are reached and which are repeated.

statement.p: For \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), find \mathbf r(\pi/3,2). Give a domain for the part with y\ge0 and height between 1 and 4.

hint.p: Use the signs of sine on [0,\pi].

solution.p: The point is (1,\sqrt3,2); one domain is 0\le\theta\le\pi, 1\le z\le4.

statement.p: Describe the grid curves of \mathbf r(u,v)=(u,v,uv) with u=c and with v=c.

hint.p: Replace the fixed parameter by the number c before interpreting the formula.

solution.p: They are the straight lines (c,v,cv) and (u,c,cu). A curved surface can contain straight lines.

exercise.title: Check the sphere and its repetitions

statement.p: For the radius-three spherical formula in , verify x^2+y^2+z^2=9. Which two edges describe the same meridian? Which edges collapse to poles?

hint.p: Use \sin^2 t+\cos^2 t=1 twice, then substitute the four boundary values.

solution.p: The sum of squares is 9\sin^2\phi(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)+9\cos^2\phi=9. The edges \theta=0,2\pi share a meridian; \phi=0,\pi collapse to (0,0,3) and (0,0,-3).

statement.p: Use the cylinder formula with 0\le z\le5. Compare the angular domains [0,2\pi] and [0,4\pi]. Do they have the same image? How many parameter pairs represent a point away from the seam in each case?

hint.p: Adding 2\pi to the angle leaves sine and cosine unchanged.

solution.p: Both describe the same cylindrical side. Away from the seam, each point occurs once in the first domain and twice in the second.

subsection.p: In , we will differentiate these grid curves one parameter at a time to find their velocities and surface normals. Surface area is developed in .
